lessons.title: Getting ready to cut cane safely
lessons.html:
Getting ready to cut cane safely

In KwaZulu-Natal and Mpumalanga many sugarcane farms still cut cane by hand. Cane cutting is hard, skilled work. Done well, it gives the mill clean cane with a lot of sugar, and leaves the stools (the roots left in the ground) healthy for the next ratoon crop.

Burnt or green cane

Some farms burn the cane before cutting to remove dry leaves (trash). Others cut green cane and leave the trash on the field to protect the soil. The farm manager decides. Burning is done only by a trained team under control, with permits where required. Never start a cane fire yourself.

Your tools

  • Cane knife: a heavy knife with a hooked or straight blade. Keep it sharp. A blunt knife needs more force and slips more easily.
  • Sharpening file or stone.

PPE

  • Leg guards or shin guards to protect your legs from the knife.
  • Strong boots.
  • Gloves to protect your hands from cane leaves and sharp stalks.
  • Safety glasses to protect your eyes from leaves and pieces of cane.
  • Long sleeves and a hat.

Look after your body

  • Drink water often. Cane cutters lose a lot of sweat. Bring a full bottle and refill it.
  • Eat a good breakfast; cutting needs energy.
  • Take short rests in the shade.
  • Tell the supervisor if you feel dizzy, sick or have cramps.

Working safely in a team

  • Keep at least two arm-and-knife lengths from the next cutter.
  • Carry the knife with the blade down, or in its cover.
  • Never swing the knife towards yourself or another person.
  • Watch out for snakes, wasp nests and holes in the field.
  • Stay clear of loaders and tractors. Make sure the driver can see you.

lessons.title: Cutting, topping and stacking the cane
lessons.html:
Cutting, topping and stacking the cane

Cutting the stalk

  1. Stand to the side of the stool with your feet apart and steady.
  2. Hold the stalks with one hand, away from where the knife will strike.
  3. Cut the stalk low, as close to the ground as you can. The bottom of the stalk has the most sugar. Low cutting also helps the stool grow back well.
  4. Do not pull or split the stool. A damaged stool gives a poor next crop.

Topping

The top of the stalk, with the green leaves, has little sugar and a lot of water. The mill does not want it. Cut the top off at the point your supervisor shows you, usually at the top of the mature, hard part of the stalk.

Cleaning (trashing)

Remove dry leaves, roots and soil from the stalk. Clean cane gives a better price. Trash, soil and stones in the load lower the payment and damage the mill.

Stacking

  • Lay the cut stalks neatly in a heap or row, all pointing the same way.
  • Keep stacks straight so the loader can pick them up easily.
  • Do not leave stalks lying all over the field; they will be lost.

Why speed matters after cutting

Cut cane starts losing sugar after it is cut, and burnt cane loses it even faster. That is why the farm plans cutting so cane gets to the mill quickly. Cut only the area you are told to cut each day.

Quality checklist

GoodBad
Cut low at ground levelHigh stumps left
Topped correctlyGreen tops left on
Clean of trash and soilSoil, roots and leaves in the stack
Neat, straight stacksStalks scattered

Look after your knife

Sharpen it during breaks, away from other people, filing away from your body. Clean and store it safely after work.

Key points

  • Wear leg guards, gloves, boots and safety glasses.
  • Keep a safe distance from other cutters and from machines.
  • Cut low, top correctly and remove trash and soil.
  • Stack neatly, all stalks the same way.
  • Cut cane loses sugar, so it must reach the mill quickly.
